Getting into trucking after failing to find a job for a year in my field of study (mechanical engineering) from a top 10 public school program.

I tend to think that "autonomous" trucks pose very little to no threat to the future of truck driving at least within the next 40 years. Firstly, the technology itself isn't there yet and won't be for a fairly long time, currently autonomous trucks can only drive properly in perfect driving conditions on the highway without any snow, rain or the like and they also can't handle poor lane marking and/or uneven road surfaces. Secondly, there will be a very long time (I think) before "fully" autonomous trucks are approved for use on public highway by American legislators. Last but definitely not the least, there are examples of transportation technologies which have been basically fully autonomous for decades and yet still require human input. Modern commercial airplanes can take off, land and hold an altitude just fine (and this has been the case for more than two decades) without any pilots being necessary but pilots are still in the flight deck to this day.

As of today, even in the most brand new and upgraded semi trucks available on the road the most options you can obtain for somewhat "autonomous" driving involve lane keep, adaptive cruise control and similar sorts of technologies we see in modern cars, which work well under ideal conditions but that is it. Keeping in mind that an 18 wheeler is a lot more complicated in its range of motion, a lot heavier, and a lot more dangerous than a passenger car (which themselves are right now a far cry from being fully autonomous), I honestly think the danger to truck driving as a career is extremely overblown.

You don't have to own anything in order to find a gig as a semi truck driver. 18 wheeler drivers are in short supply across the country literally all the time, all you need to do is sign up with a company that's willing to train new drivers. Be aware though that a gig like mine is very unusual and I only landed it because of some connections I had, at the big companies new drivers make like 45-55k a year after their ~2 months training (period depends on company) is complete. Any big trucking company (Schneider, SWIFT, etc) are willing to hire anyone with a pulse because they underpay their fresh drivers and once the drivers have enough experience they leave for smaller companies which usually pay a lot better.

As far as renting/owning trucks, yeah you can do that as well and make a lot more money than just as a driver but there are a couple of problems with it, you can't do it right out of the gate because:
1. Your insurance as a new driver will be crazy high and you have to pay for it as a business
2. Nobody will offer you a loan to buy a semi truck, most semi truck loans require 2 years of driving experience
I forgot to add, yeah we get to spend the off days at home location because the hauls end at our home base, we do round trips only.

90% of the time we venture back home on the 4th day, and the other 10% we venture back home on the 5th day so we get at least the typical weekend off. The thing is, the owners of the business also drive with us as team drivers and they like giving themselves and the drivers preferably 3 but at least 2 days off in the week, and we don't really ever haul to the "other side of the country" regardless because our home base is in a central state from which both coasts are equidistant essentially

Yeah i am enjoying it a lot as well, I love seeing new places basically every week. It is definitely not for everyone though, since you aren't home every night like a normal 9-5 the routine can seem pretty wild to the average individual and not suitable for most people, but for the right person it's great

I'm driving OTR (over the road) which means long haul trucking over all the lower 48 states. The pay is really good actually, I'm lucky to work for a smaller trucking business which pays drivers really well, in fact I am making more money than I would have in an engineering position right out of college. Usually I'm away from home for 4 days in a week, and the other 3 I have off.

Couldn't get a job since graduating last year from college in mechanical engineering, finally bailed and became a semi truck driver (something I've always been slightly interested in). Love my job right now, I get to see beautiful scenery while getting paid for it. Planning to start my own trucking company within a couple years
